title: CP-SAT assumptions as a conflict finder

blocks.text: 9.1.5 CP-SAT Assumptions as a Conflict Finder

Lesson 4.6.2 met CP-SAT's **assumptions**: guard each rule with a Boolean flag, assume every flag true, and when the model is infeasible the solver names a set of flags that cannot all hold. On GridCap small at 60% of the budget it named all 28 flags, and a deletion filter cut them to 3. The Budget Lock scenario is a different case: it has three conflicts (lesson 9.1.3), and the planners want all of them, in the rows they can change, with as few solves as possible. This lesson runs the same scenario through CP-SAT. It lists every conflict, controls which conflict a filter returns, filters whole families of rules before single rows, and finds the fewest rules to switch off. GridCap is a fictional utility; none of its numbers are real.
The Model

The model of lesson 9.1.1 with one change, marked: every row except once$`_i`$ holds only when its flag is 1. `convert.to_cpsat(model, flagged=...)` copies the MathOpt model into CP-SAT row for row, which works because CP-SAT works over the integers and all of GridCap's data are integers, and guards each named row with `.only_enforce_if(flag)`.
**Sets.** As in lesson 9.1.1, plus $`\mathcal{R}`$, the flagged rows: every row except once$`_i`$ (34 on the Budget Lock scenario). $`\leftarrow`$ new
**Parameters.** As in lesson 9.1.1, with the Budget Lock scenario's values.
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$, as before; and $`f_r \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`r \in \mathcal{R}`$: rule $`r`$ is on. $`\leftarrow`$ new
**Objective.** None for the conflict questions: each is a feasibility question, so the copy's objective is cleared. The last section maximizes $`\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} f_r`$.
**Constraints.** once$`_i`$ as in lesson 9.1.1, and every other row of that lesson guarded by its flag ($`f_r \Rightarrow \text{row } r`$):

Here $`\ell_r \le a_r^\top x \le u_r`$ is row $`r`$ of lesson 9.1.1 written with both of its bounds (one of them infinite for an inequality). For example, $`f_{\text{budget}_{2028}} \Rightarrow \sum_i \sum_t c_{i,2028-t}\, x_{i,t} \le 6{,}000`$. The **assumptions** are $`f_r = 1`$ for every $`r`$ in the set being asked about. A flag that is not assumed is a free variable, so the solver may set it to 0 and switch its rule off.
Assumptions Need Flags, One Worker and a Map From Index to Name

Lesson 4.6.2 set out the mechanics, and `conflict` here uses them unchanged. It builds the flagged copy, assumes the named flags, solves with one worker, and turns the indices the solver returns back into row names:

def conflict(assumed: list[str]) -> list[str] | None:
    """Solve with the named flags assumed true. None if feasible, else the flags the solver names."""
    global solves
    solves += 1
    model, flags = to_cpsat(lm.model, flagged=RULES)
    model.clear_objective()                           # a feasibility question
    model.add_assumptions([flags[n] for n in assumed])
    solver = cp_model.CpSolver()
    solver.parameters.num_workers = 1                 # assumptions need a single worker
    if solver.solve(model) != cp_model.INFEASIBLE:
        return None
    name = {flags[n].index: n for n in RULES}
    return [name[i] for i in solver.sufficient_assumptions_for_infeasibility()]

Three points carry over from lesson 4.6.2 and the CP-SAT troubleshooting page. `sufficient_assumptions_for_infeasibility()` returns variable indices, not names. Assumptions do not work with parallel search, hence one worker. And the set is **sufficient**: it is reduced, but not promised to be minimal. A common claim says it returns "a minimal core". The troubleshooting page does not say that, and lesson 4.6.2 measured a set of all 28 flags.
The flagged model is built afresh for every question, so that no assumption from an earlier question stays behind (`model.clear_assumptions()` would also do).
Here the Solver Named a Minimal Set at Once, So Every Conflict Costs One Solve
All 34 flags assumed:
34 flags assumed; sufficient set: 3 flags, ['crews_transmission_2030', 'crews_transmission_2031', 'must_P017']

This time CP-SAT named three flags, P017's conflict, the same three rows the reversed deletion filter found in lesson 9.1.3. How small the set comes out depends on how the solver proved infeasibility, and that changes from model to model. Here it was small. On lesson 4.6.2's scenario it was everything.
When the named sets are small, listing every conflict is cheap. Switch off one named row (one the planners set, when there is one), ask again, and repeat:

assumed = list(RULES)
while (named := conflict(assumed)) is not None:
    off = next((n for n in named if n.startswith(PLANNERS)), named[0])   # a planners' row if there is one
    print(f"named {sorted(named)} -> switch off {off}")
    assumed.remove(off)

named ['crews_transmission_2030', 'crews_transmission_2031', 'must_P017'] -> switch off crews_transmission_2030
named ['after_P023_2029', 'budget_2028', 'force_P023', 'force_P032_2028'] -> switch off budget_2028
named ['after_P023_2029', 'crews_transmission_2028', 'force_P023', 'force_P032_2028'] -> switch off crews_transmission_2028
feasible with 3 rows off (4 solves)

The three conflicts of lesson 9.1.3, in 4 solves. The HiGHS loop of that lesson needed 211: a deletion filter costs one solve per active row, and each conflict found switched one row off, so the three filters cost 70, 69 and 68 solves, plus 4 checks of whether the active rows were still infeasible (70 + 69 + 68 + 4 = 211). Each set CP-SAT named here is one of the irreducible sets that lesson found, so no filter was needed this time. Nothing promises that, so a program that reports conflicts must still check: run the deletion filter on the named set, which costs one solve per named row. On a set of 3 or 4 that is cheap. On 28 it is lesson 4.6.2's case.
<!-- practice 1 -->
The Order of a Deletion Filter Chooses Which Conflict You Get

When the named set is large, or when you want a conflict made of certain rows, run the deletion filter yourself on the flags. `minimal` is lesson 4.6.2's filter. As lesson 9.1.3 showed, it keeps the conflict whose rows come last in its order. Here it runs over all 34 flags twice, once with the rows planners set (budgets, crews, floors, overrides) first and once with them last:

for label, order in (("planners' rows tested first", theirs + model_rules),
                     ("planners' rows tested last ", model_rules + theirs)):

planners' rows tested first: ['crews_transmission_2030', 'crews_transmission_2031', 'must_P017']  (34 solves)
planners' rows tested last : ['after_P023_2029', 'crews_transmission_2028', 'force_P023', 'force_P032_2028']  (34 solves)

Tested first, the planners' rows are dropped whenever another conflict can hold without them. The 2028 rows and the overrides go, and P017's conflict survives, because its must-do row is tested late. Tested last, the must-do row is dropped early, and the conflict that survives is the overrides' one, made almost entirely of rows the planners set. For a message to the board, the second order gives the conflict they can act on. Either way the cost is one solve per flag.
Filter Whole Families First, Then the Rows Inside Them

Lesson 4.6.2's design note suggested a cheaper pass on large models: one switch per rule **family** first, then single rows only inside the families that matter. A family here is the prefix of a row's name: `budget`, `crews`, `floor`, `force`, `must`, `alt`, `after`. The first pass is a deletion filter whose items are whole families:

families: ['after', 'alt', 'budget', 'crews', 'floor', 'force', 'must'] -> needed ['crews', 'must']  (7 solves)
rows of those families: 19; minimal: ['crews_transmission_2030', 'crews_transmission_2031', 'must_P017']  (26 solves in all)

Seven solves to learn that crews and must-do rows alone are enough for a conflict, then 19 to filter the 19 rows of those two families: 26 solves against 34. The saving grows with the model: a family pass costs one solve per family, however many rows each family holds. The first pass drops the `after` family first, which is why the override conflicts (which need P023's precedence row) do not survive it. The order of the families matters just as the order of the rows did.
<!-- practice 2 -->
The Fewest Rules to Switch Off Is an Optimization, Not an Assumption

A minimal conflict answers "which rules clash?". The planners' next question is "what is the fewest rules we could drop to get a plan?". That is a different set: one that meets every conflict (it **hits** each one), rather than one conflict. Assumptions do not answer it. An objective does. Make every flag free, with no assumptions, and maximize the number of flags left on:

model, flags = to_cpsat(lm.model, flagged=RULES)
model.maximize(sum(flags.values()))
fewest rows off: 2, ['crews_transmission_2030', 'force_P032_2028']

Two rows: the 2030 transmission crews (P017 can then start in 2030) and the board's P032 override, which is in both override conflicts. The counting objective of lesson 9.1.4 also found 2, with a different pair, `must_P017` and `force_P023`. Both pairs hit all three conflicts, and the count proves no single row does. When several answers tie, a solver returns one of them, so a report should say "for example" or add a rule that breaks the tie, such as weights that make must-do rows expensive. The CP-SAT troubleshooting page makes a similar point about minimality. For a set that is truly smallest, optimize over the literals rather than rely on the sufficient set.
Summary

items: **Assumptions need flags, one worker and a map from index to name.** The set the solver names is sufficient, not promised minimal.

**Here the solver named a minimal set at once, so every conflict cost one solve:** the three conflicts in 4 solves, against 211 with HiGHS and a filter. Check a named set with a filter before reporting it as minimal.
**The order of a deletion filter chooses which conflict you get.** Put the rows you want named last. One solve per flag.
**Filter whole families first, then the rows inside them:** 7 + 19 = 26 solves instead of 34.
**The fewest rules to switch off is an optimization, not an assumption.** Maximize the flags left on. Two rows here, and the answer ties with lesson 9.1.4's.

Challenges

items: Run the "every conflict" loop switching off `named[-1]` instead of a planners' row. Predict how many conflicts it reports.
Order the family pass so that `crews` comes first. Predict which families it keeps.
Add the constraint "must-do flags stay on" to the fewest-rows model. Predict the new count.

blocks.text: Design Note: Ask the Solver for the Cheap Part, Check the Rest Yourself

CP-SAT's sufficient set costs nothing extra: it comes with the `INFEASIBLE` answer. Whether it is minimal costs one solve per member to check. A conflict finder that uses the free answer, then checks it before reporting, gets the speed of the first and the guarantee of the second. When the check finds the set already minimal, as on every set here, it has cost a few solves. When it does not, as in lesson 4.6.2, the planners never see 28 rules called "the conflict".
